questions.stem: In Han China, which crops were the staples of the north China plain and the Yangzi valley respectively?
options: Millet and wheat in the north; rice in the Yangzi valley
Rice in the north; millet and wheat in the Yangzi valley
Barley and oats in the north; maize in the Yangzi valley
Rice in both regions, grown in terraces watered by monsoon rain
questions.explanation: The dry loess lands of the north grew millet and, increasingly, wheat, while the wet south suited rice. Maize came to China from the Americas many centuries later.

questions.stem: The Western Han capital Chang'an lay in the Wei River valley, the 'land within the passes'. Why was this location attractive?
options: It lay on the coast, which allowed trade with Korea and Japan by sea
It was the old Zhou capital in the Yangzi delta, far from the Xiongnu
It was the only region of China where silk could be produced
Mountain passes made it defensible, and the valley was fertile
questions.explanation: The Wei valley, Qin's old heartland, was ringed by mountains with defensible passes and had rich irrigated farmland. It is inland, in the north-west, not on the coast or the Yangzi.

questions.stem: The Hanshu (History of the Former Han) was begun by Ban Biao, largely written by his son Ban Gu, and completed by:
options: his daughter Ban Zhao, the scholar and author of Lessons for Women
the eunuch Cai Lun, who presented it to the throne on paper
Sima Qian, who added it to the end of his Records of the Grand Historian
Emperor Guangwu, who wrote the final chapters on his own reign
questions.explanation: Ban Zhao finished parts of the Hanshu after Ban Gu's death. Sima Qian's Shiji was an earlier, separate work ending in Emperor Wu's reign.

questions.stem: Thousands of wooden slips from Han frontier posts at Juyan and Dunhuang record rations, equipment checks and messages. Their main value to historians is that they:
options: give the only surviving copy of the Confucian classics from the Han period
record the emperors' private thoughts on the Mandate of Heaven
list the names of every official in the capital for two centuries
show routine army and government work, not just court events
questions.explanation: These administrative documents were never meant for posterity, so they show routine government and soldiers' lives. The official histories focus mainly on the court and great men.

questions.stem: The Shiji and Hanshu were written by court scholars who judged rulers by Confucian moral standards. What is the most important issue this raises for historians?
options: They were written long after the Han fell, so they rely only on legend
Events may be shaped to teach moral lessons about rulers
The texts cannot be read today because Han characters have not been deciphered
Both works were written by foreign visitors who did not understand China
questions.explanation: Han historians wrote to record and to instruct, praising virtue and condemning tyranny, so their portraits can be moralised. They were contemporaries or near-contemporaries, writing in a script that is fully readable.

questions.stem: Michael Loewe described two broad attitudes in Western Han government: 'Modernists', who favoured strong state control and expansion, and 'Reformists', who favoured Confucian restraint. Which policy would a Reformist most likely oppose?
options: Appointing officials trained in the Confucian classics
Making peace with the Xiongnu instead of fighting
Keeping the state monopolies on salt and iron
Cutting taxes and spending on the imperial court
questions.explanation: Reformists criticised the monopolies and costly wars of Emperor Wu's time as burdens on the people. Lower taxes, frugality, peace and Confucian officials fit their programme.

questions.stem: The Han scholar Dong Zhongshu taught that Heaven responds to the emperor's conduct. According to this idea, an eclipse, flood or earthquake was:
options: proof that Daoist priests had cursed the imperial family
a warning from Heaven that the emperor's rule was at fault
a natural event with no meaning for the government
a sign that the emperor should begin a new military campaign
questions.explanation: Portents were read as Heaven's warnings, so officials could use them to urge reform. If misrule continued, Heaven might withdraw its Mandate and pass it to a new dynasty.

questions.stem: The emperor's title 'Son of Heaven' (Tianzi) expressed the belief that he:
options: had been chosen by election among the kings of the royal family
could never lose the throne whatever the quality of his rule
ruled by Heaven's mandate, linking Heaven and humanity
was descended by blood from the Yellow Emperor and the gods
questions.explanation: The emperor held the Mandate of Heaven and performed the great sacrifices that linked Heaven, Earth and people. The Mandate could be lost through misrule, which justified a change of dynasty.

questions.stem: From Emperor Wu's reign, each commandery was asked to recommend men as 'filial and incorrupt' (xiaolian) for office. This system:
options: chose all officials by a written examination open to every peasant
gave every office to the sons of the emperor's own relatives
allowed officials to buy their posts at a fixed price from the state
brought men of good conduct into office by recommendation
questions.explanation: Recommendation for filial piety and honesty linked Confucian values to recruitment, though in practice local elites often recommended their own. Open written examinations as the main route to office came centuries later.

questions.stem: At the top of the Western Han government, below the emperor, stood the Three Excellencies. They included:
options: the Chancellor, Imperial Counsellor and Grand Commandant
the Grand Historian, the Master of Music and the Chief Eunuch
the Empress Dowager, the Crown Prince and the Grand Tutor
the governors of the three largest commanderies of the empire
questions.explanation: The Chancellor headed the administration, the Imperial Counsellor supervised officials, and the Grand Commandant was the highest military post. The Nine Ministers ran departments below them.

questions.stem: Eunuchs served in the emperor's private quarters, while scholar-officials ran the outer court. Why did conflict between them become so bitter in the Eastern Han?
options: Officials controlled the army and refused to pay the eunuchs' salaries
Eunuchs were foreigners from the steppe who did not speak Chinese
Eunuchs near young emperors took power officials thought theirs
Eunuchs were all Daoist priests who rejected the Confucian classics entirely
questions.explanation: Living with the emperor gave eunuchs access and influence, especially under child emperors, and in 166 and 169 CE they had many officials purged. Scholar-officials saw this as a breach of proper government.

questions.stem: In 127 BCE Emperor Wu decreed that kings of the imperial family must divide their kingdoms among all their sons, not pass them to one heir. The aim was to:
options: break up the kingdoms into smaller units that could not threaten the throne
give every prince enough land to raise an army against the Xiongnu
reward the kings for their loyalty during the Rebellion of the Seven States
return the kingdoms to the descendants of the old Warring States rulers
questions.explanation: Dividing the kingdoms in each generation shrank them peacefully, continuing the reduction of royal power after 154 BCE. Commanderies run by appointed officials spread as a result.

questions.stem: Away from the capital, much real power rested with powerful local families who held land, tenants and office. For the Han state this meant that:
options: eunuchs governed the countryside directly through the Grand Commandant
officials relied on them, yet they could evade tax and resist the state
the emperor appointed every village head personally from among his own relatives
local families had no influence, since all land belonged to the state
questions.explanation: Great families helped keep order and supplied candidates for office, but they also hid land and dependants from tax. Their strength grew in the Eastern Han.

questions.stem: Several Han empresses dowager, such as Empress Lu and later Empress Dou, held great power. Their influence usually came from:
options: serving as the chief priests of the Cult of Heaven
acting for a young emperor and placing kin in office
holding the title of emperor in their own name for long periods
commanding the armies on the northern frontier in person
questions.explanation: An empress dowager could act as regent and advance her clan, the 'consort family'. Wang Mang, who founded the Xin dynasty, rose from such a family.

questions.stem: Liu Xiang's Biographies of Exemplary Women collected stories of virtuous women. Together with Ban Zhao's Lessons for Women, it shows that the Han ideal for women stressed:
options: public speaking at court on matters of state policy
obedience, chastity and devotion to husband and family
military service and leadership in local government
independence from family duties in favour of scholarship
questions.explanation: These works taught the 'three obediences', to father, husband and son, and modest conduct. Some stories also praise women's wisdom and advice, but within family roles.

questions.stem: In ordinary Han households women did most of the spinning and weaving, making cloth for the family and for sale. What does this suggest about non-royal women?
options: They had no economic role, since all cloth was made in imperial workshops
They were exempt from taxation and so had no contact with the state
They worked mainly as merchants, trading silk along the Silk Road
Their textile work was an essential part of the household and state economy
questions.explanation: The saying 'men plough, women weave' captured the ideal division of labour, and cloth sold at market helped households meet their taxes in coin. This gave women's work real economic weight, even within a patriarchal family.

questions.stem: The Five Classics studied by Han scholars and officials included:
options: the Art of War, the Han Feizi and the Book of Lord Shang
the Lotus Sutra, the Heart Sutra and the Diamond Sutra
the Book of Songs, the Book of Documents and the Spring and Autumn Annals
the Analects, the Daodejing and Sima Qian's Records of the Grand Historian
questions.explanation: The Five Classics were the Songs, Documents, Changes, Rites and Spring and Autumn Annals. The Han Feizi and Book of Lord Shang were Legalist, and the sutras are Buddhist texts that reached China later.

questions.stem: Han Confucianism stressed filial piety (xiao). In society and politics this meant that:
options: sons were expected to leave home and serve as monks in Buddhist temples
only the emperor was required to honour his ancestors with sacrifices
respect for parents and ancestors was a model for loyalty to the emperor
children could choose their own careers without consulting their parents
questions.explanation: Filial piety was the root of social order: a filial son would be a loyal subject. It was rewarded in recruitment, as the 'filial and incorrupt' category shows.

questions.stem: In the Western Han, the army was based mainly on:
options: warrior aristocrats who served for life in return for estates
volunteers from the cities who served as long as they wished
conscription of adult men for training and a period of service
hired foreign mercenaries paid in silver from the salt monopoly
questions.explanation: Commoners owed military service as well as labour, including time on the frontier. In the Eastern Han the state relied more on professional troops and non-Chinese allies.

questions.stem: On the northern frontier, Han soldiers farmed land near their garrisons in military agricultural colonies. The main purpose was to:
options: punish soldiers who had deserted by forcing them into hard labour
make frontier garrisons self-supporting and cut supply costs
train soldiers as farmers so they could leave the army after one season
grow cotton and tea for export to the Xiongnu in exchange for horses
questions.explanation: Carrying grain to distant garrisons was very costly, so soldier-farmers fed the frontier and helped hold new territory such as the Gansu corridor.

questions.stem: Which development did most to raise farm output in Han China?
options: The replacement of farming by herding livestock
Steam-powered pumps for irrigating dry fields
Wider use of iron tools and ox-drawn ploughs
The introduction of the potato from Central Asia
questions.explanation: Cast-iron ploughshares and other tools, many made in state foundries, and ox traction helped farmers cultivate more land. Potatoes and steam power belong to much later periods.

questions.stem: Under Emperor Jing the land tax was set at one-thirtieth of the harvest. Why could the Han keep the land tax this low?
options: Merchants paid all taxes, so farmers paid no tax at all
It also drew on poll taxes, labour service and other revenue
The emperor paid all government costs from his own private estates
The Han had no army or officials to pay in the early dynasty
questions.explanation: Households also paid poll taxes in coin and owed labour and military service. Later, monopolies and taxes on merchants added revenue for Emperor Wu's wars.

questions.stem: In 81 BCE officials and Confucian scholars debated the salt and iron monopolies at court, a debate later written up as the Discourses on Salt and Iron. The scholars argued that the monopolies:
options: should be handed to foreign merchants who could run them more cheaply
burdened the people with poor, costly tools and encouraged greed for profit
should be extended to silk, grain and every other product in the empire
were needed to fund new wars of conquest against the Xiongnu and Korea
questions.explanation: The literati said state profit-making was immoral and harmed farmers, while officials defended the revenue for defence. The debate shows real disagreement over the state's economic role.

questions.stem: The wuzhu ('five zhu') coin, introduced under Emperor Wu, was:
options: a round bronze coin with a square hole, minted for centuries
a gold coin with the emperor's portrait, used only for paying soldiers
a silk banknote printed by the state treasury in the capital
a cowrie shell used as money in the markets of Chang'an
questions.explanation: The wuzhu coin, named for its weight, became the standard bronze coin and was minted for about seven centuries. Chinese coins did not carry rulers' portraits, and paper money came much later.

questions.stem: Han law and Confucian thought ranked merchants below farmers and craftsmen. Which policy reflects this attitude?
options: Merchants faced heavy taxes and were barred from silk and office
Merchants were given land grants to encourage them to move to the frontier
Merchants were exempt from all taxes so they could fund the monopolies
Merchants were made the chief advisers of the emperor on all trade
questions.explanation: Early Han rules restricted merchants' dress and carriages and kept them from office, and Emperor Wu taxed their property heavily. Yet many merchants still grew rich.

questions.stem: Han lacquerware cups and boxes found in tombs often carry inscriptions naming the workshop and several workers. This evidence suggests that:
options: luxury goods came from organised workshops with divided labour
every lacquer item was made from start to finish by a single craftsman
lacquer was imported from Rome along the Silk Road and relabelled
only Buddhist monks were allowed to make lacquer for religious use
questions.explanation: Inscriptions name men responsible for different stages, such as applying lacquer, painting and inspecting, showing specialised, supervised production, some in official workshops.

questions.stem: Han smiths produced large quantities of cast iron, made by heating iron ore in furnaces hot enough to melt it, centuries before this was common in Europe. Why was this significant?
options: It meant that bronze was no longer used for any purpose in China
It allowed the Han to make coins of iron instead of bronze or gold
It made China dependent on imports of iron ore from the Roman Empire
Iron tools and weapons could be made cheaply in large numbers by casting
questions.explanation: Pouring molten iron into moulds allowed mass production of ploughshares and other goods, which the state controlled through the iron monopoly. Bronze remained in use for coins, mirrors and vessels.

questions.stem: The Han crossbow was a key weapon against the Xiongnu. Its main advantage was that:
options: a bronze trigger let ordinary soldiers shoot powerful bolts accurately
it could be fired from horseback faster than any composite bow of the steppe
it used gunpowder to fire bolts much further than any other weapon
it was so light that it replaced the sword and spear entirely
questions.explanation: A precisely made bronze lock held the drawn string and released it with a trigger, so infantry with little training could shoot strongly. Gunpowder weapons came many centuries later.

questions.stem: Zhang Heng, an Eastern Han official and scholar, is famous for designing:
options: an instrument to detect distant earthquakes
the first printed book with movable type
a magnetic compass for ships at sea
a water clock to time the imperial exams
questions.explanation: Zhang Heng's seismoscope of 132 CE was said to indicate the direction of a distant earthquake. Movable type and the ship's compass came much later.

questions.stem: The Queen Mother of the West (Xiwangmu), often shown on Han tomb reliefs and mirrors, was worshipped as:
options: the goddess of the harvest, honoured at the spring ploughing ceremony
a demon who punished the souls of the dead for their crimes
a goddess of a western paradise who could grant immortality
the ancestor of the Han royal house, honoured in the imperial temple
questions.explanation: Xiwangmu was linked with the peaches of immortality and a western paradise, and her cult spread widely among ordinary people in the late Western Han.

questions.stem: Emperor Wu performed the feng and shan sacrifices at Mount Tai in 110 BCE. These rites were meant to:
options: report to Heaven and Earth that the dynasty had brought peace
mourn the soldiers who had died in the wars against the Xiongnu
consult the oracle bones about the choice of the next heir
celebrate the arrival of Buddhism from India by building a temple
questions.explanation: The feng and shan were rare, grand sacrifices reporting a ruler's achievements to Heaven and Earth. The First Emperor had also performed them, and Buddhism arrived later in the Eastern Han.

questions.stem: Han thinkers explained change in nature and history through yin and yang and the Five Phases. The Five Phases were:
options: air, fire, earth, water and spirit
jade, silk, bronze, iron and salt
sky, mountain, river, forest and sea
wood, fire, earth, metal and water
questions.explanation: The Five Phases succeeded one another in cycles, and each dynasty was linked to a phase. Air, fire, earth and water belong to the Greek system of elements.

questions.stem: In Han practice, the Book of Changes (Yijing) was used mainly for:
options: teaching soldiers the use of the crossbow and the spear
divination, using yarrow stalks to build hexagrams
recording the annual taxes owed by each household in the commanderies
training scholars in the laws and punishments of the Han code
questions.explanation: The Yijing's 64 hexagrams were interpreted to give guidance, and it was also one of the Five Classics. Divination informed decisions from family matters to state affairs.

questions.stem: Many Han Chinese believed a person had two souls. At death, the hun and the po:
options: were both reborn at once as an animal, as Buddhist teaching held
were judged by Osiris and either rewarded or destroyed
joined together to guard the family's house as a door god
parted, the hun rising to heaven and the po staying with the body
questions.explanation: The po remained in the tomb and needed food and goods, while the hun could travel to the realm of the immortals or ancestors. This helps explain richly furnished tombs and ancestral offerings.

questions.stem: Tombs of the Marquis of Dai's family at Mawangdui contained a T-shaped silk banner showing heaven, the human world and the underworld, along with food, clothes and silk books. What does this burial best show about Han beliefs?
options: The family rejected the afterlife and buried only items they no longer wanted
Burial goods were offerings to the Buddha to win rebirth in a western paradise
Only emperors were thought to have an afterlife, so the tomb was purely symbolic
The dead were believed to need provisions and guidance for a journey after death
questions.explanation: The banner from Lady Dai's tomb seems to show her journey, and the goods supplied her life in the tomb. Mawangdui dates from the early Western Han, before Buddhism reached China.

questions.stem: Prince Liu Sheng and his wife Dou Wan were buried at Mancheng in suits made of thousands of jade plaques sewn with gold wire. The suits reflect the belief that jade could:
options: show that the couple had been Daoist priests
pay the tax owed by the dead to the underworld
prove the couple had been merchants in life
preserve the body and protect it from decay
questions.explanation: Jade was believed to have protective, preserving power, though the bodies inside had decayed by the time of excavation. Such suits were reserved for royalty and the highest nobles.

questions.stem: Early Han tombs were usually vertical pits with wooden chambers; by the Eastern Han many were brick or stone chambers laid out like houses, with carved scenes of daily life. What does this change suggest?
options: The tomb was increasingly imagined as a home for the dead, like a dwelling
Wood had become unavailable across all of China during the Han dynasty
Burial was abandoned for cremation, so tombs were built for display only
Buddhism forbade the use of wooden coffins in tombs from 25 CE
questions.explanation: House-like chambers, models of granaries and towers, and reliefs of banquets show the tomb as a dwelling for the po. These changes reflect belief, not a shortage of timber.

questions.stem: Sima Qian's Shiji is organised into sections that include:
options: laws, statutes, ordinances, judgements and model legal cases
dialogues between Confucius and his disciples on good conduct
basic annals, tables, treatises, hereditary houses and biographies
odes, hymns, ballads, laments and songs from the Music Bureau
questions.explanation: The Shiji's 130 chapters combine annals of rulers, chronological tables, treatises on topics such as rites and the economy, accounts of noble houses, and biographies. Later dynastic histories copied this form.

questions.stem: Sima Xiangru is famous for the fu, or rhapsody. This form of Han literature is best described as:
options: prose histories of the dynasty written in the form of annals
moral dialogues between a teacher and his students on virtue
long, ornate descriptive verse-prose praising splendour
short four-line poems describing nature in very simple language
questions.explanation: The fu piles up rich vocabulary and description, as in Sima Xiangru's pieces on hunting parks. It often ends with a moral note urging restraint, though its splendour can overwhelm the lesson.
